planting.note: Divide established clumps or plant nursery starts in spring once soil has warmed, in humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled to full shade.

directions: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, siting it where its stiff, leathery, deeply lobed fronds can be appreciated up close. Unlike the more common Japanese holly fern, this species carries a distinctive fishtail-shaped terminal pinna at the tip of each broad, coarsely toothed leaflet, giving the whole frond a bold, sculptural silhouette that reads well against finer-textured shade companions. It tolerates brief dry spells and a bit more sun than many woodland ferns once established, but performs best with consistent moisture and protection from harsh afternoon exposure. Cut back tattered fronds in late winter to make way for the flush of glossy new growth each spring.

common_name: Dwarf Japanese Holly Fern (Coastal Holly Fern)

planting.note: Set divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; use as a low edging fern rather than a specimen since its fronds hug the ground.

directions: Grow in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, giving it room to spread as a dense, low mat rather than an upright clump. This naturally occurring coastal variety of Japanese holly fern stays remarkably flat and compact, with glossy, dark holly-like leaflets lying close to the soil surface instead of arching upward, making it useful as a textured groundcover or rock-garden edger where a taller holly fern would look out of scale. It shares the species' tolerance for salt spray, wind, and cold better than most evergreen ferns, holding its color through winter in protected sites. Groom out old or browned fronds occasionally to keep the low mat looking fresh.

common_name: Arching Japanese Holly Fern (Cliff Holly Fern)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, along slopes or edges where the arching habit can be shown off.

directions: Site in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, ideally on a slope, bank, or raised bed where its fronds can arch outward and downward as they do on the hillsides it grows on in the wild. Native to shaded, damp roadcuts and hillsides in China and Japan, this compact variety of Fortune's holly fern produces shorter, more horizontally held fronds with pale yellow-green, glossy pinnae than the straight species, giving it a softer, more graceful presence in small woodland gardens and containers. It is markedly more cold-hardy than the tropical Japanese holly fern and holds its foliage through winter in most of its range. Remove old or damaged fronds at the base in early spring before new growth emerges.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in full shade with high ambient humidity; best treated as a terrarium or frost-free groundcover plant rather than a hardy outdoor perennial.

directions: Grow in constantly moist, humus-rich soil in full shade with elevated humidity, since dry air quickly browns the delicate frond tips. This cultivar of Krauss's spikemoss forms a dense, creeping mat of fine, moss-like foliage tipped in creamy white to soft yellow, giving the mat a frosted, dusted appearance that is especially striking massed under other shade plants or in a terrarium. It has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for its dependable performance in cool, shaded, humid conditions. Where winters are too cold for outdoor use, grow it in a humidity tray, closed terrarium, or shaded container that can be moved under cover, and divide congested mats in spring to renew vigor and increase stock.
